title: Chapter 14.  New Status — Jammu and Kashmir & Ladakh as Separate Union Territories

blocks.content: This chapter details the structural, administrative and territorial specifics of the 2019 bifurcation — precisely what the new J&K UT and the new Ladakh UT each look like, which districts/areas went where, and how their administrative frameworks differ from one another.
The Two New Union Territories Compared

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 reconstituted the state into two distinct Union Territories: Jammu & Kashmir, and Ladakh.
The UT of Jammu and Kashmir is provided with a Legislative Assembly, whereas the UT of Ladakh is administered directly by the Centre without a legislature.
Ladakh comprises the two districts of Leh and Kargil, while the UT of Jammu and Kashmir encompasses the remaining 20 districts.
A common High Court continues to function as the judicial authority for both Union Territories.

blocks.content: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 bifurcated the state into two Union Territories: Jammu & Kashmir, and Ladakh.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: J&K UT (with Assembly) and Ladakh UT (without Assembly) is one of the most fundamental and frequently tested structural facts of the post-2019 landscape — do not describe J&K and Ladakh as having identical administrative structures; they are meaningfully different in exactly this one critical respect.
Territorial Composition of the New J&K UT

items: The new UT of Jammu and Kashmir comprises the former state's Jammu division and Kashmir division in their entirety, EXCLUDING the Leh and Kargil districts, which were carved out to form the separate UT of Ladakh.

This means J&K UT retains the historically 'Jammu and Kashmir' core identity — the Jammu plains/Shivalik zone, the Pir Panjal, and the Kashmir Valley (all covered in the Geography chapters) — while Ladakh UT takes the historically distinct, high-altitude Trans-Himalayan Leh and Kargil districts, whose own geography (Karakoram, Ladakh Range, Indus valley) was outlined in Chapter 2 as adjacent-but-administratively-separate context.

The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 also carried consequential amendments extending numerous central laws to the new UT and repealing/adapting the erstwhile J&K state's own separate laws (including its separate Ranbir Penal Code, later replaced by the applicable central criminal codes, and its separate land and property laws, several of which were substantially amended to remove Article 35A-linked restrictions).

blocks.content: Key Legal & Administrative Changes Introduced by the Reorganisation

items: J&K UT possesses a Legislative Assembly provisions under Article 239A, similar to Puducherry, whereas Ladakh is a UT without a legislature.
The official appointed date for the enforcement of the reorganisation was 31st October 2019 (National Unity Day).
Parliamentary representation allocates 5 Lok Sabha seats and 4 Rajya Sabha seats to J&K UT, while Ladakh gets 1 Lok Sabha seat and 0 Rajya Sabha seats.

cells: A new 'domicile' category was introduced by subsequent rules, defined more broadly than the old Permanent Resident category (covering, among others, those who have resided in the UT for a specified period, or whose parents/children meet specified residence or government-service criteria), replacing the Article 35A framework for eligibility for local government jobs and certain other benefits

Restrictions on the purchase of land/property by non-residents that had existed under the old Permanent Resident framework were substantially removed, opening the UT's real-estate and land market to a wider pool of Indian citizens, a change welcomed by proponents as boosting investment and criticised by opponents as risking altering the region's demographic and land-ownership character

Central reservation norms (for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, and Economically Weaker Sections) were extended to J&K in line with the rest of India, alongside specific J&K-focused reservation categories for residents of areas along the international border/LoC and for certain other specified local categories

J&K's earlier separate Ranbir Penal Code and related procedural codes were repealed and replaced by the applicable central codes extended to the rest of India (and subsequently by India's newer central criminal-law codes as those came into force nationally)

items: J&K UT: 20 districts, 90-seat Assembly + 5 nominated members, elected CM/Council of Ministers since Oct 2024.
Ladakh UT: 2 districts (Leh, Kargil), NO Assembly, administered solely by an LG.
Ladakh's inclusion under the Constitution's Sixth Schedule remains an active, unresolved political demand (prominently associated with activist Sonam Wangchuk).
'Domicile' status (post-2019) replaced 'Permanent Resident' status (pre-2019, under Article 35A) as the basis for local job/benefit eligibility, with broader qualifying criteria.
Land-purchase restrictions on non-residents were substantially removed; central reservation categories (SC/ST/OBC/EWS) extended to J&K, alongside specific border-area reservation categories.
